title: Light as Wave and Ray
description: Two complementary pictures of how light behaves

concepts.title: The Ray Model
concepts.contentHtml:
For most everyday optics, we can treat light as a ray — a straight line traveling at speed c through a uniform medium.

This works because light's wavelength (≈500 nm for visible) is tiny compared to the lenses, mirrors, and apertures we typically use. Geometric optics — reflection, refraction, image formation — falls out of the ray picture alone.

The model fails when objects approach the wavelength scale: that's when diffraction and interference take over.

concepts.title: The Wave Model
concepts.contentHtml:
Light is also an electromagnetic wave — oscillating electric and magnetic fields propagating through space.

The frequency f and wavelength λ are linked by c = fλ. Visible light spans roughly 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red), but the spectrum extends from radio waves (km) to gamma rays (sub-pm).

Wave behavior dominates whenever you set up two coherent sources or pass light through a slit narrower than the wavelength.

concepts.title: Wave-Particle Duality
concepts.contentHtml:
Light is also a stream of photons — discrete energy packets with E = hf, where h is Planck's constant.

The photoelectric effect (Einstein 1905) showed that low-frequency light cannot eject electrons no matter how bright, because each photon must individually have enough energy.

Modern optics uses whichever picture is convenient: rays for camera design, waves for diffraction, photons for detector counts. They are all the same thing.

title: Reflection, Refraction & Lenses
description: How light bends and how images form

concepts.title: Snell's Law
concepts.contentHtml:
When light crosses a boundary between two materials, it bends. The amount of bending is set by the refractive index n of each medium, with n = c/v (speed in vacuum divided by speed in the medium).

Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Light slows down going into glass (n ≈ 1.5) and bends toward the normal. The deeper bend at lower speed is exactly the same principle that makes a marching band turn when one row hits mud.

concepts.title: Total Internal Reflection
concepts.contentHtml:
When light tries to leave a denser medium (high n) for a thinner one, there's a critical angle beyond which it can't escape — it reflects entirely back.

This is why fiber optic cables work: light bounces along the core, never leaking out, carrying internet across oceans. It's also why a diamond sparkles — its high index (n ≈ 2.4) traps light inside, bouncing repeatedly before escaping in concentrated flashes.

concepts.title: The Thin Lens Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
A lens uses refraction to bend parallel rays toward (converging) or away from (diverging) a focal point.

For a thin lens, the object distance d_o, image distance d_i, and focal length f are linked by 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f.

This single equation describes cameras, microscopes, telescopes, and the human eye. Magnification = -d_i/d_o; the negative sign tracks whether the image is inverted.

title: Interference & Diffraction
description: Wave optics — what happens when light meets itself

concepts.title: Young's Double Slit
concepts.contentHtml:
Pass coherent light through two narrow slits and you get a pattern of bright and dark fringes on a screen — proof that light is a wave.

Where path lengths from the two slits differ by a whole wavelength, crests align and you get a bright fringe (constructive interference). Differ by a half wavelength and you get cancellation (destructive interference).

Young's 1801 experiment killed Newton's pure-corpuscle theory of light. A century later, doing it with electrons proved they are waves too.

concepts.title: Single-Slit Diffraction
concepts.contentHtml:
Even a single slit spreads light into a pattern, because every point inside the slit acts as a tiny secondary wavelet (Huygens' principle).

The first dark fringe occurs at sin θ = λ/a, where a is the slit width. Narrower slits produce wider patterns. Cameras have finite apertures, so this sets a fundamental resolution limit.

concepts.title: Diffraction Gratings
concepts.contentHtml:
A grating with thousands of slits sharpens the interference pattern dramatically. Each wavelength gets sent in its own narrow direction, splitting white light into a clean spectrum.

Astronomers use gratings to measure star compositions; chemists use them in spectrophotometers. The colors on a CD or DVD are diffraction off the closely spaced data tracks.

title: Polarization & Lasers
description: Aligning the wave — and amplifying it coherently

concepts.title: Polarization
concepts.contentHtml:
Light's electric field oscillates perpendicular to the direction of travel — but the oscillation direction can be horizontal, vertical, or anything between.

A polarizing filter passes only one direction. Sunglasses cut glare because reflected light off horizontal surfaces is preferentially horizontally polarized; a vertical polarizer blocks it.

Crossed polarizers stop almost all light. Slip a clear strip of stressed plastic between them and watch the rainbow — that's birefringence revealing internal stress.

concepts.title: Stimulated Emission
concepts.contentHtml:
Einstein showed (1917) that an excited atom can be triggered by an incoming photon to emit a second photon — identical in wavelength, direction, and phase.

Set up a medium where most atoms are excited (a population inversion) and put it between mirrors, and one stray photon kicks off a cascade: each new photon stimulates more, all coherent, all aligned.

That's how a laser works. The acronym: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

concepts.title: Why Lasers Are Different
concepts.contentHtml:
Ordinary light from a bulb is incoherent — random phases, broad spectrum, spreading in all directions.

Laser light is coherent: all photons in phase, same wavelength, same direction. That's why a laser pointer makes a tiny dot a kilometer away and why interferometers use lasers — coherence preserves phase information across long distances.

Lasers cut steel, perform eye surgery, read DVDs, run fiber-optic networks, and detected gravitational waves at LIGO.

title: Modern Photonics
description: Holograms, fiber optics, and the photonic future

concepts.title: Holography
concepts.contentHtml:
A photograph records intensity. A hologram records phase too — encoding the full wavefront from the object.

You make one by interfering an object beam (light scattered off the subject) with a reference beam on a film. Replaying the reference beam reconstructs the original wavefront — your eye sees the 3D object as if it were really there.

Real-time holographic displays are an active research frontier. Holographic data storage and security holograms (on credit cards, banknotes) are already practical.

concepts.title: Fiber Optics
concepts.contentHtml:
An optical fiber is a hair-thin glass strand with a higher-index core and lower-index cladding. Total internal reflection traps the light in the core, and it travels for kilometers with minimal loss.

Modern long-haul fibers can carry tens of terabits per second per fiber. The internet is, almost entirely, photons in glass.

Wavelength-division multiplexing sends many colors down the same fiber simultaneously, each as an independent channel.

concepts.title: Quantum & Nonlinear Optics
concepts.contentHtml:
At high intensities, materials respond nonlinearly: shine infrared light (1064 nm) into a crystal and out comes green (532 nm, frequency doubling). This is how green laser pointers work.

Quantum optics manipulates single photons — entangled pairs, squeezed states, photon blockade. These are the building blocks of quantum cryptography (BB84) and emerging photonic quantum computers.

Metamaterials and photonic crystals engineer light's behavior at the wavelength scale, enabling perfect lenses, cloaking demonstrations, and slow light.
